**The Cartographer of Forgotten Places**

Mira collected places the way some people collected stamps or coins. Not postcards or photographs—actual places, with their soil and stone and the particular way the light fell at certain hours.

Her apartment was small, but the walls were lined with maps she'd drawn by hand. Not of the world as it was, but of the world as it had been, and sometimes as it might become. There was a map of the street where her grandmother had lived before the highway came through, complete with the old oak tree that had stood for two hundred years. There was a map of the forest path she used to walk to school, now buried beneath a shopping center, but the path was there in her ink, winding faithfully between imaginary trees.

People thought her strange. *"Why dwell on what's gone?"* they'd ask, and she'd smile and say nothing, because how could she explain that the gone places were the most real ones? The present was always slipping, always becoming memory even as you stood in it. The past, at least, had the dignity of staying put.

One winter, she heard about a town called Vellburn that was about to be flooded. A new reservoir. The whole valley would be underwater by spring.

She packed her bags and took the train.

Vellburn was smaller than she'd expected, and quieter. The kind of place where everyone knew your business before you did, and the church bells still rang at noon even though half the pews were empty. She rented a room above the post office from a woman named Greta, who fed her soup and asked no questions.

For three weeks, Mira walked every street. She sketched the library with its leaning porch. She drew the old mill, the schoolhouse with the bell that hadn't rung in decades, the cemetery on the hill where four generations of Vellburns lay beneath weathered stones. She measured nothing precisely; this was not survey work. This was an act of devotion.

On her last evening, she sat with Greta on the porch. The sun was going down in a way that made the whole valley look like it was on fire.

"You're trying to save it," Greta said. Not a question.

"No," Mira said. "I'm trying to remember it. So that someone, somewhere, will know it was here."

Greta was quiet for a long time. Then she said, "There's a girl in town. Orphan girl, about nine. She's been watching you. Says she wants to learn."

Mira turned. Across the street, half-hidden behind a lilac bush, a small face peered out—wide eyes, dirty knees, a look of fierce concentration.

"What's her name?"

"Lily."

Mira thought about all the maps on her walls. All the places she'd preserved in ink, alone in her apartment. The thought that any of it might continue after her had never really occurred to her. She had assumed, in some quiet way, that the collection would end with her—that the forgotten places would return to being forgotten, just one more room of things no one visited anymore.

She looked at Lily. Lily looked back.

"Mira," she called softly. "Come here. I'll show you where to start."

The child crossed the street slowly, as if approaching something wild.

And on the porch, in the last of the light, three generations sat together as the valley prepared to sleep, and then to disappear, and then, in some small way, to be kept.
